name: Clomiphene

track.title: Lab & animal
track.line: Rat fertility studies on the label

track.title: FDA approval
track.line: Clomid, 1967, ovulation in women. Men: off-label

what.text: Clomiphene citrate is a non-steroidal drug that acts on estrogen receptors. It is a mix of 2 forms (isomers): zuclomiphene, 30% to 50%, and enclomiphene. The label says the 2 forms have mixed estrogen-like and anti-estrogen effects.
How it acts, according to the FDA label:

items.text: It competes with estrogen at estrogen receptors in the hypothalamus, pituitary and reproductive organs.

The first effect is a rise in the pituitary’s release of gonadotropins (LH and FSH). In women this leads to growth of an ovarian follicle and ovulation. In men, higher LH and FSH tell the testes to make more testosterone; the label does not describe this.

src.label: Guay et al., J Clin Endocrinol Metab

items.text: It has no apparent progestogen, androgen or anti-androgen effects.

what.text: Clomiphene is approved only for ovulation problems in women who want to become pregnant. Its use in men, for low testosterone or infertility, is off-label.

research.text: Clomid was approved on trials in women; the label counts 7,578 women. In men, small randomized trials show that clomiphene raises LH, FSH and testosterone. A large WHO trial found no effect on male infertility, and trials found little or no change in sexual function.

research.title: WHO trial in idiopathic male infertility

facts.v: multicentre, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled
190 couples; the man had poor semen quality of unknown cause
clomiphene citrate 25 mg a day or placebo
6 months; 1,308 couple-months studied
pregnancy rates, semen quality

research.found: Pregnancy rates at 8 months were 11.7% on placebo and 8.1% on clomiphene. Semen quality changed no differently between groups. The authors found no evidence that clomiphene treats this kind of male infertility.

research.title: Men with erectile dysfunction and secondary hypogonadism (Guay et al.)

facts.v: double-blind, placebo-controlled, crossover
17 men with erectile dysfunction and low testosterone from the pituitary (secondary hypogonadism)
2 months on clomiphene and 2 months on placebo
LH, FSH, total and free testosterone; sexual function by questionnaire and night-time erection testing

research.found: LH, FSH and testosterone rose on clomiphene compared with placebo. Sexual function did not improve, except for some limited measures in younger, healthier men.

src.label: Guay et al., J Clin Endocrinol Metab

research.title: Clomiphene vs anastrozole in infertile men with low testosterone (Helo et al.)

facts.v: randomized, prospective, double-blind comparison (no placebo)
26 infertile men with testosterone under 350 ng/dL and normal LH
clomiphene citrate 25 mg a day or anastrozole 1 mg a day, both off-label
12 weeks
hormones, semen analysis, erectile function and androgen-deficiency questionnaires

research.found: Testosterone rose in both groups, more on clomiphene (mean rise 571 vs 408 ng/dL). Estradiol rose on clomiphene and fell on anastrozole. Neither group changed semen measures or questionnaire scores.

src.label: Helo et al., J Sex Med

research.title: Obese men with low testosterone (Soares et al.)

facts.v: single-center, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled
78 men, mean age 36.5, with a BMI over 30 and low testosterone from the pituitary
clomiphene citrate 50 mg or placebo
12 weeks
symptom and sexual questionnaires, hormones, body composition, lipids, blood vessel function, PSA, hematocrit

research.found: On clomiphene, total and free testosterone, estradiol, LH, FSH and SHBG rose, and lean and muscle mass rose. One sexual complaint (weaker erections) improved. HDL (good) cholesterol fell. Blood vessel function did not change.

src.label: Soares et al., Int J Obes

research.title: Clomiphene or enclomiphene in male hypogonadism (Hohl et al.)

facts.v: systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized trials up to July 2024
men with functional hypogonadism in trials against placebo, testosterone gel or hCG
total testosterone, LH, FSH

research.found: Compared with placebo, the drugs raised total testosterone by a mean 274 ng/dL, with LH and FSH also higher. Testosterone did not differ from testosterone gel. The trials varied a lot (I² up to 89%).

src.label: Hohl et al., Arch Endocrinol Metab

research.text: In the clinical studies behind the label, about 30% of women became pregnant. 7.98% of pregnancies were multiple. These data say nothing about effects in men.
In male rats, clomiphene by mouth lowered fertility at low doses and caused temporary infertility at higher doses. Long-term cancer studies in animals have not been done.

us.text: Clomiphene citrate is FDA approved, first as Clomid in 1967, only to treat ovulation problems in women who want to become pregnant. Use in men is off-label. It is not a controlled substance. As of November 1, 2026.

items.text: NDA 016131 (Sanofi), approved February 1, 1967, is now listed as discontinued. The Clomid brand is still marketed under ANDA 075528 (Cosette), and several generic tablets are approved, the newest in 2026.

items.text: treatment of ovulatory dysfunction in women desiring pregnancy.

off-label. The label states there are no adequate or well-controlled studies showing that clomiphene treats male infertility, and that testicular tumors and breast growth have been reported in men taking it. It does not say the tumors were caused by the drug.

under section 503A, pharmacies may compound only with bulk substances that meet a USP or NF monograph, are part of an FDA-approved drug, or are on FDA’s 503A bulks list. Clomiphene citrate is the active ingredient of FDA-approved tablets. A compounded clomiphene product is not FDA approved.

world.lead: Clomiphene (clomifene) is an approved fertility medicine for women in the US, Northern Ireland and 20 EU member states. Canada’s database lists no marketed product: every clomiphene product there is cancelled. Use in men is off-label wherever checked. It is banned in sport at all times.

countries.status: Approved medicine (Clomid, 1967; generics) for ovulation problems in women. Prescription-only. Use in men is off-label.

after.text: Australia’s Poisons Standard (October 2026) lists clomifene in Schedule 4 (prescription only) and in Appendix D, clause 1: for human use it may be supplied only by, or on the prescription of, an authorised medical practitioner. The TGA’s register could not be reached to confirm which products are registered.

after.title: Sport
after.text: Clomifene is named under class S4.2, anti-estrogenic substances (anti-estrogens and SERMs), on the WADA 2026 Prohibited List. S4 is prohibited at all times (in and out of competition), and S4.2 substances are Specified Substances. The ban is not limited to men. Clomifene stays named in S4.2 on the 2027 list, in force January 1, 2027, where the class title adds estrogen receptor degraders (SERDs).

side.text: The label’s side effects come mostly from women treated for infertility: ovarian enlargement, hot flushes, visual symptoms that can rarely be lasting, ovarian hyperstimulation, and multiple pregnancy. In men, the label notes reports of testicular tumors and breast growth; trials in men found a fall in HDL cholesterol.

items.text: blurring, spots or flashes can occur and become more common with higher total dose or longer use. They usually go away, but prolonged and possibly irreversible cases have been reported. The label says anyone with visual symptoms should stop and have an eye exam.

in clinical studies (8,029 women), the most common were ovarian enlargement (13.6%), hot flushes (10.4%), abdominal or pelvic discomfort (5.5%), nausea and vomiting (2.2%), breast discomfort (2.1%), visual symptoms (1.5%) and headache (1.3%).
ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome can progress fast and become serious, with fluid in the abdomen and lungs, blood clots and, rarely, death.
testicular tumors and breast growth (gynecomastia) have been reported in men; a causal link is not known.
in a 12-week trial in obese men, HDL cholesterol fell on clomiphene.

items.text: after approval, reports included heart rhythm problems, pulmonary embolism, stroke, seizures and skin reactions. A link to the drug could not always be established.
it must not be used in pregnancy or by people with liver disease. In male rats it lowered fertility.

The Clomid label itself says no adequate or well-controlled studies show that clomiphene treats male infertility, and a WHO trial in 190 couples (1992) found no benefit on pregnancy rates.
